content: Ovarian carcinoma is the seventh most common cancer affecting women globally and is the leading cause of death from gynecological cancers in Europe and North America. Despite numerous studies investigating chemotherapy for this disease, most individual trials have been too small to definitively establish the superiority of any specific chemotherapy regimen. The type and intensity of chemotherapy used for women with advanced ovarian cancer have varied due to uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of different treatment regimens. This review aimed to compare the efficacy of single-agent chemotherapy versus combination regimens, platinum-based chemotherapy versus non-platinum-based chemotherapy, and carboplatin-based regimens versus cisplatin-based regimens in women with advanced ovarian cancer. To gather data, researchers conducted searches in the MEDLINE and CancerLit bibliographic databases, as well as in trial registers maintained by the National Cancer Institute and the UK Co-ordinating Committee on Cancer Research. They also manually reviewed conference proceedings and reached out to experts in the field and pharmaceutical companies for additional information. The review included randomized trials that compared the following treatment regimens in women with advanced ovarian cancer: 1. Single-agent non-platinum chemotherapy versus non-platinum combination chemotherapy. 2. Single-agent non-platinum chemotherapy versus platinum-based combination chemotherapy. 3. Non-platinum regimens versus the same regimens with the addition of cisplatin. 4. Single-agent platinum chemotherapy versus platinum-based combination chemotherapy. 5. Cisplatin-based chemotherapy versus carboplatin-based chemotherapy. Data from these trials were collected directly from the investigators, verified by the reviewers, and cross-checked with the trial investigators. A total of 49 trials involving 8,763 women were included in the analysis. The data were pooled to calculate hazard ratios (HR) for survival, analyzed on an intention-to-treat basis. For single-agent non-platinum chemotherapy compared to platinum-based combination chemotherapy, the overall hazard ratio (HR) for survival was 0.93 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.83 to 1.05), slightly favoring platinum-based combination therapy. When non-platinum regimens were compared to the same regimens with the addition of cisplatin, the HR for survival was 0.88 (95% CI: 0.79 to 0.98), indicating a survival benefit from adding platinum to the regimen. Comparing single-agent platinum chemotherapy to platinum-based combination chemotherapy yielded an HR of 0.91 (95% CI: 0.79 to 1.05), favoring combination therapy. For cisplatin versus carboplatin-based chemotherapy, the HR was 1.02 (95% CI: 0.93 to 1.12), showing no significant difference between the two platinum agents. Subgroup analyses were conducted for cisplatin versus carboplatin, examining factors such as age, cancer stage, tumor grade, histology, extent of surgical resection, residual tumor burden, and performance status. No significant differences in treatment effects were observed across these subgroups. In conclusion, the available evidence, while not definitive, suggests that platinum-based chemotherapy is more effective than non-platinum-based therapy for advanced ovarian cancer. There is also some evidence that combination chemotherapy improves survival compared to single-agent platinum therapy. However, no significant difference in efficacy was found between cisplatin and carboplatin.
